title: Bono: Gold at the Edge of the Forest

pages.text: Go to Techiman on a market day. Lorries stand in long lines, loaded with yams, maize, tomatoes, and cashew. Traders have come from Kumasi and Tamale, and also from Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger. You will hear Twi, Hausa, Dagbani, French, and more. Techiman is one of the busiest food markets in West Africa, because it sits where the forest meets the savanna and the roads from north and south cross. This is not new. Six hundred years ago, traders met in the same country. But they had not come for yams. They had come for gold.

pages.text: A short way north of Techiman lay Bono Manso, the capital of the Bono kingdom. Many historians count Bono as one of the earliest Akan states, growing strong from about the 1300s or 1400s. Its own tradition says that the first Bono people came out of a hole in the ground at a place called Amowi. Stories like this are a people’s way of saying: we have always belonged here. The king was called the Bonohene. His land had two great gifts. It had gold in its streams and soil, and it stood on the road between two different worlds.

pages.text: To the north lay the great markets of the River Niger, such as Jenne and Timbuktu. Camel caravans carried goods from there across the Sahara desert to North Africa. Those markets wanted gold. Muslim traders known as the Wangara came south with donkeys loaded with salt, cloth, and brass. The Bono had gold and also kola nuts from the forest. A trading town named Begho grew up in Bono country, with separate quarters for local people, for visiting merchants, and for craftsmen. Archaeologists who dug there found brass, beads, and broken pots from far away.

pages.text: How do you buy and sell with gold dust? You must weigh it. Bono traders used small scales and sets of brass weights, and they agreed on fixed units so that nobody was cheated. The weights were small works of art, cast in the shapes of fish, birds, drums, and symbols that stood for proverbs. A trader’s bag of weights showed both wealth and learning. Using them needed quick arithmetic with fractions. The skill of working gold and brass spread from Bono to other Akan peoples. The goldsmiths of later kingdoms learned from this tradition.

pages.text: Wealth draws envy. By the early 1700s, a new power had risen in the forest to the south: Asante. Around 1722 to 1723, the Asante army under King Opoku Ware marched north and captured Bono Manso. The Bono king was taken to Kumasi, and the old capital was never rebuilt. Asante gained more than treasure. Bono goldsmiths, weavers, and officials carried their knowledge to the Asante court. The Bono people gathered again around Techiman, which became their new centre. A kingdom can lose a war and still pass on its skills.

pages.text: The name lives on. In 2019, two of Ghana’s new regions were called Bono and Bono East. Each year, in Techiman and Wenchi, people celebrate the Apoo festival. For several days, anyone may sing openly about wrongs done in the past year, even wrongs done by chiefs, and no one may punish them for it. It is an old way of clearing the air and keeping leaders honest. The lesson of Bono is plain. A people who stand at a crossroads, trade fairly, and measure honestly can grow rich without conquering anyone.

activities.question: Why was the Bono kingdom so well placed for trade?
options: It was on the sea coast
It lay between the forest and the savanna, on the road linking north and south
It was hidden deep in the forest where no one could reach it

activities.question: What did the Wangara traders bring south to exchange for gold and kola?
Why did traders need brass weights?
options: To weigh gold dust fairly using agreed units

activities.question: Apply it: During Apoo, people may criticise their leaders without punishment. Which modern idea is closest to this?
options: Freedom of speech and holding leaders to account

activities.prompt: Put these events in order, from earliest to latest.
items: The Bono kingdom grows strong at Bono Manso
Wangara traders come south and Begho becomes a busy trading town
The Bono people gather again around Techiman
Two regions of Ghana are named Bono and Bono East
